claims.quote: the much more practicable thing is that upper footpath, with these moving platforms beside it, running out over the street after the manner of the viaduct of an elevated railroad.
claims.description: City streets will gain elevated footpaths with moving platforms (travelators) running beside them.

claims.quote: the demonstrated cheapness and practicability of tunnels at a considerable depth will come into play.
claims.description: Deep, cheap tunnels will be used to carry urban transit traffic underground.

claims.quote: the process of elimination that is beginning now with the heavy vans spreading until it covers all horse traffic, and with the disappearance of horse hoofs and the necessary filth of horses, the road surface may be made a very different thing
claims.description: Horse traffic will disappear from city streets, leaving cleaner, better-drained road surfaces for motor hackney vehicles and cyclists.

claims.quote: there is no reason but the existing filth why the roadways should not have translucent *velaria* to pull over in bright sunshine and wet weather.
claims.description: City roadways could be covered by retractable translucent awnings to shield from sun and rain.

claims.quote: this diversion of the vast omnibus traffic of to-day into the air and underground, together with the segregation of van traffic to specific routes and times
claims.description: Omnibus traffic will be moved above and below ground and freight vans restricted to set routes and times.

claims.quote: An easily portable substance, which could be decomposed electrically by wind or water power, and which would then recombine and supply force, either in intermittent thrusts at a piston, or as an electric current, would be infinitely more convenient for all locomotive purposes than the cumbersome bunkers and boilers required by steam.
claims.description: A portable chemical energy-storage substance (like a fuel or battery medium) charged by wind or water power will replace steam for transport.

claims.quote: Their advent will be the beginning of the end for steam traction on land and of the steam ship at sea: the end indeed of the Age of Coal and Steam.
claims.description: Explosive/storage-of-force engines will end the age of coal and steam power for land and sea transport.

claims.quote: There can be little doubt that the sea speeds of 50 and even 60 miles an hour will be attained within the next few years.
claims.description: Turbine-driven ships will reach sea speeds of 50 to 60 miles per hour.

claims.quote: There is hardly any reason, beyond this tradition of the horse, why the railway carriage should not be even nine or ten feet wide, the width, that is, of the smallest room in which people can live in comfort, hung on such springs and wheels as would effectually destroy all vibration
claims.description: Railway carriages could be built much wider, vibration-free, and furnished like comfortable rooms.

claims.quote: the happy suggestion (for the ferry transits, at any rate) of a rail along the sea bottom, which would serve as a guide to swift submarine vessels, out of reach of all that superficial "motion" that is so distressing, and of all possibilities of collision.
claims.description: Submarine vessels guided by a rail along the sea bottom could provide fast ferry crossings.

claims.quote: But I do not think it at all probable that aeronautics will ever come into play as a serious modification of transport and communication—the main question here under consideration.
claims.description: Flying will not become a serious mode of transport or communication.

claims.quote: I have supposed the replacement to occur in the case of the London Inner Circle Railway
claims.description: Existing rail lines will be replaced by moving-platform transit systems.

claims.quote: not only will many of these railway-begotten "giant cities" reach their maximum in the commencing century, but that in all probability they, and not only they, but their water-born prototypes in the East also, are destined to such a process of dissection and diffusion as to amount almost to obliteration
claims.description: Giant cities will peak and then diffuse across the countryside so thoroughly that they nearly vanish as concentrated urban blots.

claims.quote: It is much more probable that these coming cities will not be, in the old sense, cities at all; they will present a new and entirely different phase of human distribution.
claims.description: Future cities will not be dense cities but a diffused, new pattern of human settlement.

claims.quote: the London citizen of the year 2000 a.d. may have a choice of nearly all England and Wales south of Nottingham and east of Exeter as his suburb, and that the vast stretch of country from Washington to Albany will be all of it "available" to the active citizen of New York and Philadelphia before that date.
claims.description: Fast commuting will let city workers live in suburbs hundreds of miles away, covering most of southern England or the US East Coast corridor.

claims.quote: a circle with a radius of thirty miles gives an area of over 2800 square miles
claims.description: Suburban railways at thirty miles an hour will make a 30-mile radius commutable for daily workers.

claims.quote: So far as London, St. Petersburg, and Berlin go, it seems fairly safe to assume that they will go well over twenty millions; and that New York, Philadelphia, and Chicago will probably, and Hankow almost certainly, reach forty millions.
claims.description: Diffused metropolitan regions will reach populations of twenty to forty million.

claims.quote: the available area for the social equivalent of the favoured season-ticket holders of to-day will have a radius of over one hundred miles, and be almost equal to the area of Ireland.
claims.description: Faster transit will give well-off commuters a 100-mile radius for daily travel.

claims.quote: it is a distinct promise of a centrifugal application that may be finally equal to the complete reduction of all our present congestions.
claims.description: New transport technology will relieve urban congestion by pushing population outward.

claims.quote: this "Democracy," or Wholesale method of living, like the railways, is transient—a first makeshift development of a great and finally (to me at least) quite hopeful social reorganization.
claims.description: Mass uniform living will give way to a more individualized social reorganization.

claims.quote: The picture of this swarming concentrated humanity has some effective possibilities, but, unhappily, if, instead of that obvious rule-of-three sum, one resorts to an analysis of operating causes, its plausibility crumbles away
claims.description: The expectation of ever-larger, densely packed megacities with tenements and moving ways is rejected as implausible.

claims.quote: The great city cannot grow, except as a result of some quite morbid and transitory process—to be cured at last by famine and disorder—beyond the limit the commercial capacity of that commanded area prescribes.
claims.description: Each city's population is capped by the commercial capacity of its hinterland, and growth beyond that would end in famine and disorder.
